title: The Holy Land
hookLine: walking where Jesus walked, and praying for its people

lines: DAWN ON THE SEA OF GALILEE.
cards: A pilgrim kneels in a low cave under a church in Bethlehem and touches a silver star set into the floor.
Days later she stands on the shore of the Sea of Galilee at dawn: fishing boats, gulls, the same water the Gospels keep returning to.
Then Jerusalem: narrow stone streets, a shopkeeper calling out, a bell, a call to prayer. She has read these names her whole life. Nazareth.
Capernaum. Gethsemane. Now they're under her feet, with weather, traffic and neighbors.

teach.b: For Christians, what makes this land holy goes back to John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Flesh means a body, and a body stands somewhere.
Jesus was born in one town, grew up in another, fished and taught by a particular lake, and died outside a particular city wall.

teach.h: THE GROUND AS A FIFTH GOSPEL.
teach.b: Some people call the land itself the fifth gospel. The four are written down; the fifth, they say, is the ground: the hills, the distances, the water.
Walking from the lake up into the hills, a pilgrim can feel how far Jesus walked, and why his stories are full of fishermen, sheep and seeds. Next, the shrines.

Churches stand over the places tradition links to the Gospel story: the grotto of the Nativity in Bethlehem, the Annunciation in Nazareth, and in Jerusalem the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, over the place of the crucifixion and the tomb.
Franciscan friars care for many of these shrines on behalf of Catholics. Then, the people. The Holy Land is not a museum.

teach.h: NOT A MUSEUM: PEOPLE LIVE THERE.
teach.b: Christian families live there, some in towns their families have called home for generations. Jews and Muslims hold places in the same land holy too, and live and pray there.
Catholic pilgrims are encouraged to pray for everyone who lives there, and for peace.
Last, the living stones. Pilgrims sometimes say the shrines are the old stones, and the local Christians are the living ones. Both are part of the visit.

how: Catholics make pilgrimages to the Holy Land, often in parish groups led by a priest, celebrating Mass at shrines such as Bethlehem, Nazareth and the Holy Sepulchre; the Church also asks Catholics to pray and give for the Christians who live there and for peace in the region.

games.q: you're on pilgrimage in Bethlehem. your group has an hour free. what do you do with it?
o: go back to the grotto for one more photo.
visit a local Christian family's shop and talk with them.
games.why: any of these is fine, but pilgrims are encouraged to meet the living stones: the Christians who live in the land now.

practice: Picture one street in Jerusalem or Bethlehem in the morning: a Christian grandmother opening her shutters, a Jewish father walking his children to school, a Muslim shopkeeper sweeping his step, children everywhere.
Don't sort them; hold them all together, their safety, their work, their sleep tonight. If you pray, say Lord, have mercy, once for each; if you don't, wish them peace, one by one.

wordCard.voice: The Holy Land. The places where Jesus was born, lived, died and rose, visited by pilgrims as a kind of fifth gospel, and home to people of more than one faith. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek of John 1:14: the Word became flesh, the line that makes the land holy for Christians.

carryVoice: Your line: the fifth gospel. The ground the Gospels walked on still has neighbors. See you tomorrow.
